column3: It repeats the focus closing formula exactly: accumulated gains fail to avail their owners.

Qarun explicitly says he received wealth through his own knowledge, while earlier wealthier generations were destroyed; it is the clearest precedent for the focus's inherited claim.
Qarun's wealth and dwelling are swallowed up, and no faction can help him, concretely exposing the failure of acquired security.
Those who had desired Qarun's position recognize that provision is God's to expand or restrict and that denial does not prosper.
The owner of abundant gardens is left with ruined property and no supporting group, a concrete reversal of self-secure wealth.
The garden owner enters his estate wronging himself and assumes it will never perish, articulating the confidence later overturned.
He treats wealth and followers as proof of superior return, making explicit the security inference denied by the focus.
Rival accumulation distracts people, identifying an earlier formative dynamic behind confidence in gain.
Worldly life is described as rivalry in wealth and children followed by withering, framing acquisition as transient rather than protective.
It warns that wealth and children can distract from God's remembrance, a related limit on material preoccupation.
Opponents cite greater wealth and children as grounds for immunity from punishment, a direct version of the false security claim.
It explicitly denies that wealth and children bring people near to God, directly rejecting material status as protection.
People who desire Qarun's worldly portion display the social attraction of the wealth that will shortly prove unable to protect him.
Those given knowledge answer the desire for Qarun's status by distinguishing God's reward from mere accumulated wealth.
The garden owner claims greater wealth and a stronger following, supplying the status claim overturned in the same narrative.
After the garden's ruin he has neither supporting faction nor help, completing the failure of his acquired security.
The conclusion assigns all protective authority and best outcome to God rather than to the estate's owner.
It compares present people with earlier communities who had greater strength, wealth, and children yet consumed their allotted share and perished.
It questions whether provision of wealth and sons should be read as a hastening of good, directly challenging prosperity as a verdict.
It completes the question of whether expanding wealth and sons means that good is being hastened for their owners.
It warns against being impressed by wealth and children because they can become a means of punishment rather than security.
It states that wealth and children will not avail their possessors against God, a close formulation omitted from the list.
It again denies that wealth and children will avail anyone against God, applying the warning to a specific opposing group.
It identifies wealth and children as a test, qualifying their apparent value without directly stating their failure to avail.
It names the day when neither wealth nor sons will avail, giving the focus's warning its final temporal setting.
On the day of judgment, even close relations cannot protect one another, dismantling another presumed source of security.
It includes all possessions on earth in the imagined ransom that still cannot rescue its owner.
The human being treats expanded provision as proof of honor, directly exposing the prosperity inference behind the focus's claim.
He treats restricted provision as humiliation, showing the same false reading of material condition from the opposite side.
The hoarder who counts accumulated wealth embodies confidence in possession that the surrounding warning overturns.
It explicitly says the amassed wealth is thought to make its owner immortal, an extreme form of the failed-security claim.
It identifies transgression with seeing oneself as self-sufficient, supplying the underlying disposition of the inherited saying.
It calls wealth and children the adornment of worldly life while giving lasting deeds the better value.
